extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing 35 U.S.C. §101 patent-eligibility analysis using the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 1, 2A, 2B), including how to identify judicial exceptions and when claims may be eligible as improvements to computer functionality or other technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non‑statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the BRI encompasses non‑statutory embodiments (e.g., machine‑readable media that can encompass transitory carrier waves), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is appropriate. It is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to embodiments that fall within a statutory category. See examples (In re Nuijten; Mentor Graphics v. EVE‑USA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Claim must fall within statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) (Step 1: YES); if clearly not within one of the four categories (Step 1: NO), reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting under Step 1, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 per MPEP §706.03(a). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant’s disclosure indicates the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to determine whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C and recommend amendment if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (and related terms such as products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes), and these are not patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no bright lines between types of exceptions; many concepts can fall under multiple exceptions. For eligibility analysis it is sufficient for the examiner to identify that the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception) aligns with at least one judicial exception. See cited Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (Alice, Myriad, Mayo, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern is underlying but not sole test
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of judicial exceptions is driven by the concern about preemption—patents should not monopolize basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is inherent in and addressed by the Alice/Mayo two‑part framework (Steps 2A and 2B); preemption is not a standalone test. Examiners should apply the Alice/Mayo test because absence of complete preemption does not itself demonstrate eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Directed to a judicial exception (recite vs involve)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea — i.e., whether such an exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim. A claim is directed to an exception when that exception is recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different language ('set forth' vs 'describe') indicates different ways an exception may be recited. Examiners must consider the claim as a whole and distinguish between claims that recite an exception (require further analysis at Step 2B) and claims that merely involve or are based on an exception (eligible and do not require further analysis). Examples: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' (recites law of nature → Step 2A: YES) versus a teeter‑totter claim that merely involves the law of the lever (Step 2A: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of multiple or parsed exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions unless clearly distinct; steps that manipulate information via a series of mental steps should be treated as a single abstract idea for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites multiple exceptions (even if not distinct), it is directed to at least one judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and thus requires further analysis at Step 2B. See RecogniCorp v. Nintendo as example where multiple abstract ideas led to Step 2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to determine if a claimed concept is an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (specific claim limitation(s) believed to be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing the claimed concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to previously identified abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES). If it is not similar and there is no basis to conclude it is an abstract idea, find that the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO) and eligible at Pathway B unless it recites another exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality/technology are not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inventions that claim improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract and therefore may be eligible at Step 2A (or via streamlined Pathway A), provided they are appropriately claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit examples include Enfish (self‑referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization using rules), and Visual Memory (enhanced memory system). Examiners must give the claim its BRI, evaluate specification and claim together, and require that the specification disclose sufficient detail so a person of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. The claim itself must reflect the improvement (covering a particular solution or way to achieve an outcome rather than the mere idea). See MPEP §2106.05(a) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claimed improvement is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim does not reflect an improvement to computer‑functionality or technology if the claimed process can be performed without a computer, if it merely automates conventional activity, or if improvements arise solely from using a general‑purpose computer or conventional components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit authorities (e.g., Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance; Affinity Labs; TLI Communications) indicate that mere automation, speed increases due only to generic computers, or conventional implementation on generic components are insufficient to show an improvement. Examiners should consult MPEP §2106.05(a) for cases and further examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvements early and consider in full Alice/Mayo analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim improves computer functionality or other technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis, since such an improvement may render the claim eligible at Pathway A or Pathway B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvement is clear (e.g., Enfish), the claim could be found eligible at Pathway A under a streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not directed to an abstract idea. If not clear in Step 2A, the improvement may still contribute to eligibility in Step 2B. See MPEP §2106.06(b) and §2106.05(a).
